chapter.name: Alternating Current
chapter.blurb: The chapter studies circuits driven by a sinusoidal ac voltage: a resistor, an inductor and a capacitor separately, with rms values, reactances and the phase relation between current and voltage shown by phasors. It then solves the series LCR circuit by the phasor diagram to obtain the impedance and phase angle, and treats resonance and the average power with its power factor. It ends with the transformer and its use in the transmission of electrical energy.

concepts.name: AC voltage applied to a resistor and the phasor picture
concepts.description: A sinusoidal voltage across a pure resistor, the in-phase current it drives, the instantaneous and average power, and the representation of ac quantities by phasors.
concepts.idea: In a pure resistor the alternating current rises and falls exactly in step with the alternating voltage, and although the current averages to zero over a cycle the heating does not.
concepts.rule: An ac source gives v = vm sin(omega t), where vm is the amplitude (peak value) and omega the angular frequency. Applied to a resistor R, Kirchhoff's loop rule gives i = im sin(omega t) with im = vm/R, which is Ohm's law and holds for ac as for dc. Voltage and current reach their zero, maximum and minimum values at the same instants: they are in phase (phase angle zero). Over one complete cycle the average current is zero, but the instantaneous power p = i^2 R = im^2 R sin^2(omega t) is never negative; since the average of sin^2(omega t) over a cycle is 1/2, the average power is (1/2) im^2 R. A phasor is a vector that rotates about the origin with angular speed omega; its magnitude is the peak value and its vertical component is the instantaneous value of the quantity. For a resistor the V and I phasors point in the same direction at all times. Voltage and current are scalars; phasors are only a convenient way of adding sinusoidal quantities. AC is preferred for supply mainly because ac voltages are easily and efficiently changed by transformers.
concepts.example: v = 120 sin(50 t) volt across 40 ohm gives i = 3 sin(50 t) ampere; the average power is (1/2) x 3^2 x 40 = 180 W.

concepts.name: RMS values and average power in a resistor
concepts.description: The root mean square (effective) current and voltage, their relation to peak values, and the average power written in the dc form.
concepts.idea: The rms value of an alternating current is the steady direct current that would heat the same resistor at the same average rate.
concepts.rule: The rms or effective current is I = sqrt(mean of i^2) = im/sqrt(2) = 0.707 im, and the rms or effective voltage is V = vm/sqrt(2) = 0.707 vm. In terms of rms values V = I R, and the average power is P = I^2 R = V^2/R = I V, the same forms as for dc. It is customary to quote rms values for ac: the household line voltage of 220 V is an rms value, with peak value sqrt(2) x 220 = 311 V. The power rating of an element used in ac circuits is its average power. The ac ampere is defined through Joule heating, a property independent of the direction of the current: an alternating current has an rms value of one ampere if it produces the same average heating as one ampere of direct current under the same conditions.
concepts.example: A bulb rated 100 W for a 220 V (rms) supply has R = 220^2/100 = 484 ohm and carries an rms current of 100/220 = 0.454 A.

concepts.name: AC voltage applied to an inductor
concepts.description: The current driven through a pure inductor by an ac source, inductive reactance, the phase lag of the current and the zero average power.
concepts.idea: A pure inductor limits an alternating current through its reactance, which grows with frequency, and makes the current lag the voltage by a quarter cycle without consuming any power on average.
concepts.rule: For a pure inductor (negligible winding resistance) connected to v = vm sin(omega t), the loop rule gives v - L di/dt = 0, so i = im sin(omega t - pi/2) with im = vm/XL. The inductive reactance is XL = omega L = 2 pi f L; it has the dimension of resistance, its SI unit is the ohm, and it is directly proportional to the inductance and to the frequency. The same relation holds for rms values: I = V/XL. The current lags the voltage by pi/2, that is by one-quarter of a cycle (it reaches its maximum T/4 later). The instantaneous power is p = -(im vm/2) sin(2 omega t), whose average over a complete cycle is zero, so the average power supplied to a pure inductor is zero. Inserting an iron rod into a coil increases its inductance and hence its reactance; a bulb in series with it then glows less brightly.
concepts.example: A 0.10 H pure inductor on a 110 V (rms), 50 Hz source has XL = 2 x 3.14 x 50 x 0.10 = 31.4 ohm and carries an rms current of 110/31.4 = 3.5 A.

concepts.name: AC voltage applied to a capacitor
concepts.description: The current in a purely capacitive ac circuit, capacitive reactance, the phase lead of the current and the zero average power.
concepts.idea: A capacitor blocks a steady direct current once charged but passes an alternating current by charging and discharging every half cycle, with the current a quarter cycle ahead of the voltage.
concepts.rule: In a dc circuit a capacitor carries current only for the short time needed to charge it; when fully charged the current is zero. On an ac source v = vm sin(omega t) the capacitor is alternately charged and discharged, so it limits but does not prevent the flow of charge. With q = C v and i = dq/dt, i = omega C vm cos(omega t) = im sin(omega t + pi/2), where im = vm/XC. The capacitive reactance is XC = 1/(omega C) = 1/(2 pi f C); it has the dimension of resistance, its SI unit is the ohm, and it is inversely proportional to the frequency and to the capacitance. The same relation holds for rms values: I = V/XC. The current leads the voltage by pi/2, reaching its maximum one-quarter of a period earlier. The instantaneous power is p = (im vm/2) sin(2 omega t), which averages to zero over a complete cycle. A lamp in series with a capacitor does not glow on dc; on ac it glows, and less brightly if C is reduced.
concepts.example: A 15.0 micro-F capacitor on a 220 V (rms), 50 Hz source has XC = 1/(2 pi x 50 x 15.0 x 10^-6) = 212 ohm and carries an rms current of 220/212 = 1.04 A.

concepts.name: Series LCR circuit: impedance and phase angle
concepts.description: The phasor-diagram solution of a series LCR circuit: adding the voltages across R, L and C with their phases to obtain the impedance and the phase angle between source voltage and current.
concepts.idea: In a series LCR circuit the same current flows through all three elements, and their voltages must be added as phasors, not as plain numbers.
concepts.rule: In a series LCR circuit driven by v = vm sin(omega t) the current i = im sin(omega t + phi) is the same in R, L and C at every instant. The voltage across R is in phase with the current, the voltage across L is pi/2 ahead of the current and the voltage across C is pi/2 behind it, with amplitudes vRm = im R, vLm = im XL, vCm = im XC. The phasors VL and VC lie along the same line in opposite directions, so vm^2 = vRm^2 + (vCm - vLm)^2. Hence im = vm/Z with impedance Z = sqrt(R^2 + (XC - XL)^2), and the same holds for rms values, I = V/Z. The phase angle is given by tan phi = (XC - XL)/R; the impedance diagram is a right-angled triangle with sides R and (XC - XL) and hypotenuse Z. If XC > XL, phi is positive, the circuit is predominantly capacitive and the current leads the source voltage; if XC < XL, phi is negative, the circuit is predominantly inductive and the current lags. Rms voltages across elements cannot be added algebraically: in an RC circuit V = sqrt(VR^2 + VC^2). The phasor method gives only the steady-state solution; a transient solution also exists and dies out after a sufficiently long time.
concepts.example: With R = 3 ohm, XL = 8 ohm and XC = 4 ohm, Z = sqrt(3^2 + (8 - 4)^2) = 5 ohm and tan phi = (4 - 8)/3, so phi is negative and the current lags the source voltage.

concepts.name: Resonance in a series LCR circuit
concepts.description: The resonant frequency of a series LCR circuit, the minimum impedance and maximum current at resonance, and applications such as radio tuning and metal detectors.
concepts.idea: At one particular frequency the inductive and capacitive reactances cancel, the impedance drops to R alone and the current is as large as it can be.
concepts.rule: As omega is varied, at omega0 the reactances are equal, XC = XL, i.e. 1/(omega0 C) = omega0 L, so the resonant angular frequency is omega0 = 1/sqrt(LC) and the resonant frequency is omega0/(2 pi). At resonance the impedance is minimum, Z = R, the current amplitude is maximum, im = vm/R, and the current is in phase with the source voltage. The voltages across L and C are equal and opposite in phase and cancel, so the total source voltage appears across R. Resonance needs both L and C: it cannot occur in an RL or an RC circuit. For the same L and C a smaller R gives a larger current at resonance, at the same resonant frequency. In tuning a radio the capacitance of the tuning circuit is varied until its resonant frequency nearly equals the frequency of the wanted station. A metal detector doorway is a coil and capacitor tuned to resonance; metal changes the impedance and hence the current, which triggers the alarm.
concepts.example: With L = 0.5 H and C = 20 micro-F, omega0 = 1/sqrt(0.5 x 20 x 10^-6) = 1/sqrt(10^-5) = 316 rad/s; at this frequency XL = XC = 158 ohm, so Z = R and the current is as large as it can be.

XL = omega0 L = 100 x 2 = 200 ohm and XC = 1/(omega0 C) = 200 ohm, so VL = VC = 4 x 200 = 800 V. These two are equal and opposite in phase, so the drop across the LC combination is 800 - 800 = 0, and the whole source voltage appears across R.

questions.q: The frequency of the ac source connected to a series LCR circuit is slowly raised from well below the resonant frequency to well above it, the voltage amplitude being kept fixed. questions.a: Below resonance XC = 1/(omega C) is larger than XL = omega L, so the circuit is predominantly capacitive and the current leads the source voltage; as the frequency rises XC falls and XL rises, the impedance decreases and the current amplitude grows. Above resonance XL exceeds XC, the circuit is predominantly inductive and the current lags; the impedance increases again and the current amplitude falls.

At resonance XC = XL - Z = R is minimum, the current amplitude vm/R is maximum, in phase
Above resonance XL > XC - current lags, impedance rises and the current falls

With only R and L there is nothing to cancel the inductive reactance at any frequency, so the impedance is always greater than R and no resonance is possible.

s: C = 1/(omega0^2 L) = 1 nF
Peak current at resonance = vm/R = 0.2 A
For 2.0 x 10^6 rad/s, C = 0.25 nF

concepts.name: Power in an ac circuit and the power factor
concepts.description: The average power in a series LCR circuit, the power factor cos phi, wattless current, and why a low power factor wastes power in transmission.
concepts.idea: Only the part of the current that is in phase with the voltage delivers power, so the average power is the product of rms voltage and rms current reduced by the power factor.
concepts.rule: For v = vm sin(omega t) and i = im sin(omega t + phi) the instantaneous power is p = (vm im/2)[cos phi - cos(2 omega t + phi)]; the time-dependent term averages to zero, so the average power is P = V I cos phi = I^2 Z cos phi, with V and I rms values. cos phi is the power factor, and from the impedance triangle cos phi = R/Z. Resistive circuit: phi = 0, cos phi = 1, maximum power dissipation. Purely inductive or purely capacitive circuit: phi = pi/2, cos phi = 0, no power is dissipated although a current flows; this is called wattless current. In an RL, RC or LCR circuit power is dissipated only in the resistor, P = I^2 R. At resonance XC = XL, phi = 0, cos phi = 1 and P = I^2 R is maximum. The power consumed in an ac circuit is never negative. For supplying a given power at a given voltage a low power factor needs a larger current and so causes a larger I^2 R loss in transmission; with a lagging current the power factor is improved by connecting a capacitor of suitable capacitance in parallel, whose leading wattless current cancels the lagging wattless component.
concepts.example: With R = 3 ohm, XL = 8 ohm, XC = 4 ohm and an rms current of 40 A, Z = 5 ohm, the power factor is 3/5 = 0.6 and P = I^2 R = 40^2 x 3 = 4800 W.

s: R = 80 ohm and net reactance 60 ohm
I = 2 A (rms) and P = 320 W
Make XL = XC (net reactance zero) so that Z = R and the power factor is 1

concepts.name: Transformers
concepts.description: The principle and construction of a transformer, the voltage and current relations of an ideal transformer, step-up and step-down action, energy losses and the use of transformers in power transmission.
concepts.idea: A transformer changes an alternating voltage by mutual induction: the voltages are in the ratio of the turns, and what is gained in voltage is given up in current.
concepts.rule: A transformer has a primary coil of Np turns and a secondary coil of Ns turns, insulated from each other and wound on a soft-iron core. An alternating voltage on the primary produces an alternating flux that links the secondary and induces an emf in it (mutual induction): es = -Ns d(phi)/dt and ep = -Np d(phi)/dt. For an ideal transformer (negligible primary resistance, all the flux linking both coils, small secondary current) vs/vp = Ns/Np. If it is 100 per cent efficient, ip vp = is vs, so ip/is = vs/vp = Ns/Np; that is Vs = (Ns/Np) Vp and Is = (Np/Ns) Ip, also for rms values. Ns > Np gives a step-up transformer (higher voltage, smaller current); Ns < Np gives a step-down transformer (lower voltage, larger current). Energy losses in an actual transformer: flux leakage (reduced by winding the coils one over the other), resistance of the windings (I^2 R heat, reduced by thick wire in high-current windings), eddy currents in the core (reduced by a laminated core) and hysteresis (reduced by a core material with low hysteresis loss). A well designed transformer may have an efficiency of more than 95 per cent. For long-distance transmission the generator voltage is stepped up so that the current and the I^2 R loss are reduced, and stepped down again near the consumers.
concepts.example: With Np = 300 and Ns = 900, a 110 V (rms) input at 6 A is stepped up to a 330 V output at 2 A.
